sections.h: The letters to Egypt in 2 Maccabees
sections.b: 2 Maccabees opens with two letters from Judea urging the Jews of Egypt to keep the feast of the temple's purification on 25 Kislev (2 Maccabees 1:1–9; 1:10–2:18). The first, dated 124 BC, calls it "the Feast of Booths in the month of Kislev"; the book later explains that the first celebration was kept for eight days like the Feast of Booths, which the fighters had missed (2 Maccabees 10:6). The second letter gives the feast a history: the fire of the first temple, hidden at the exile and found again by Nehemiah, and Solomon's eight days of dedication (2 Maccabees 1:18–36; 2:9–12). Josephus calls the feast "Lights" (Antiquities 12.325), and the rabbis tell of oil that burned for eight days (Bavli Shabbat 21b).

common: Most scholars accept the first letter of 2 Maccabees (1:1–9) as a genuine festal letter of 124 BC.
uncommon: Ben Zion Wacholder argued that the second letter (1:10b–2:18) is a genuine letter from Judas's lifetime.

sections.b: 2 Maccabees opens its history with Onias III as the ideal high priest: the laws were kept "because of the godliness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of evil" (2 Maccabees 3:1). He defends the temple deposits of widows and orphans against Heliodorus, then offers a sacrifice to save Heliodorus's life (3:10–12, 31–33). His brother Jason buys the office from him (4:7–10), and he is murdered near Antioch at Menelaus's order (4:33–35). Many scholars find him in Daniel's "anointed one" who is cut off (Daniel 9:26).

sections.b: A letter in 2 Maccabees says that Jeremiah, warned by God, took the tent, the ark and the altar of incense to Mount Nebo and sealed them in a cave, saying the place would stay unknown "until God gathers his people in" (2 Maccabees 2:4–8). The Lives of the Prophets and the Orthodox synaxarion for 1 May tell the same story; 2 Baruch 6 has an angel hide the vessels, and the rabbis say Josiah hid the ark (Bavli Yoma 52b). Jeremiah's own book says the ark will no longer be remembered (Jeremiah 3:16), and John sees it in God's temple in heaven (Revelation 11:19).

A letter at the start of 2 Maccabees makes Nehemiah the builder of the temple and the altar and tells how his priests found the altar's fire, hidden at the exile, as a thick liquid that burst into flame (2 Maccabees 1:18–36). It also says he founded a library of "the books about the kings and prophets, and David's books" (2:13). The book of Ezra gives the temple's rebuilding to Zerubbabel and Jeshua (Ezra 3:2; 6:15), and Sirach praises Nehemiah for the walls (Sirach 49:13).

2 Maccabees 2:13–15 says Nehemiah gathered "the books about the kings and prophets, and David's books, and letters from kings about gifts," and that Judas gathered again what the war had scattered. With the prologue to Sirach and Luke 24:44, it is among the earliest texts to speak of Israel's sacred books in groups. Roger Beckwith used it to argue that the Hebrew canon was settled early; others reply that it describes a collection, not a closed list.

sections.h: The horseman and the young men
sections.b: In 2 Maccabees 3 a horse with a rider in golden armor and two splendid young men drive Heliodorus from the temple treasury; later the young men appear again and tell him he owes his life to the high priest's prayer (2 Maccabees 3:24–34). The book returns to such "appearances" in battle (5:2–4; 10:29–30; 11:8). Angels appear as young men in Tobit 5 and at Jesus' tomb (Mark 16:5).

In 2 Maccabees 3 God defends the Jerusalem treasury against Heliodorus, who confesses that "he who has his home in heaven is himself the overseer and helper of that place" (3:39). Two chapters later Antiochus IV robs the temple unharmed, and the writer explains that "the Lord did not choose the nation for the sake of the place; he chose the place for the sake of the nation" (5:19). The two stories set out the book's view of the temple: holy, guarded by God, but sharing the fortunes of its people.
